- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Dropbox
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## Core Behavior

- Prioriti… [truncated]

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- add-backlinks: Add backlinks from related blog posts and glossary entries to a target post. Use when the user wants to improve internal linking by having other content link back to a specific article.
- blog-post: Create or revise a blog post for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to write a new blog post, revise/refresh an existing one, or update content. Guides through gathering information, content structure, internal linking, and post-publish steps.
- evergreen-posting: Generate a batch of evergreen social media posts (LinkedIn / Mastodon / Bluesky) promoting the AI Failure Modes quiz and existing blog posts / glossary entries. Use when Mark says "create posts", "schedule social media", "draft an evergreen batch", or asks for N days of social content. Outputs a single JSON file the posting pipeline can consume, and marks the source calendars so the same content isn't promoted twice.
- glossary-entry: Create a new glossary term for the Agile Pain Relief website. Use when the user wants to add a new Agile/Scrum term definition, concept explanation, or methodology entry to the glossary.
- indexing-strategy: Use this skill when Mark asks to analyze, plan, or implement SEO topic clusters and internal linking for agilepainrelief.com. Covers two modes: (1) ANALYZE mode — audit existing content, identify pillar/cluster opportunities, find gaps and orphaned pages, and produce a prioritized action plan; (2) IMPLEMENT mode — generate specific internal linking instructions, write or revise blog posts and glossary entries to fit the cluster strategy, and produce per-page checklists. Also use when Mark asks what a blog post or glossary entry needs for SEO, or when he wants to check whether a draft meets the cluster linking requirements.
- newsletter: Draft and send a newsletter to the Newsletter Subscribers list via Cakemail, starting from plain markdown. Use when Mark wants to write, render, test, or dispatch a newsletter / email campaign, or turn a markdown file into a Cakemail draft campaign. Drives the email-automation CLI's send-newsletter command.
- social-media-adapt: Adapt LinkedIn posts to Mastodon and Bluesky formats with platform-specific character limits, thread formatting, and JSON structure. Use when Claude needs to convert LinkedIn content to other social platforms, create threaded posts, or adapt content for different character limits (Mastodon 500 chars, Bluesky 290 chars).
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

10	# Quiz C: draft copy (for Mark to rewrite in his own voice)
11	
12	**What this is:** a complete first draft of every piece of copy for Concept C, cover to follow-up emails. It's my attempt at your voice, not the final word. Rewrite freely; the design decisions underneath (five questions, concrete-recall anchoring, safe-to-admit honest answers, honest-middle result, no badge, no invented benchmark, reclaim-then-redirect move, well-positioned fallback) are the parts to preserve.
13	
14	**Placeholders to fill:** the course name and links are marked `[[like this]]`. I've left the course as a placeholder because the brand-voice doc has it in flight (Pragmatic AI for Agile Teams).
15	
16	**Note on the result:** it's dynamic, so I've written it as a shared scaffold plus a small library of component sentences the page assembles from your answers, then shown two fully worked examples so you can see a real result end to end.
17	
18	---
19	
20	## 1. The landing page (cover)
21	
22	**Headline (working, under 15 words):**
23	Where is your Scrum Master role heading in an AI world?
24	
25	**Subhead (under 25 words):**
26	Five honest questions about how you actually spent last week. See which parts of your role are gaining value, and which are quietly slipping away.
27	
28	**The reassurance line:**
29	This isn't a personality quiz. There's no flattering label at the end. Just an honest read of where your work is going, and one thing to do about it.
30	
31	**What you'll get (3 bullets):**
32	- A map of last week: the work that's rising in value, and the work a tool will soon do instead of you.
33	- Your single highest-leverage move, the one change worth making first.
34	- No archetype, no score to frame on the wall, nothing you can't act on.
35	
36	**The opt-in:**
37	Where should I send your result?
38	[ email field ]
39	Button: **Show me my map**
40	
41	Small print under the button: No spam. Unsubscribe anytime.
42

45	## 2. The five questions
46	
47	Each question is anchored in a specific, recent memory (not "in general"), and the unflattering answer is written to be safe to pick.
48	
49	### Q1. Where the week actually went
50	
51	Think back over last week. When you look at where the hours really went, what took up most of them?
52	
53	- **a)** Running the ceremonies and keeping the board and reports up to date. Honestly, that was most of it.
54	- **b)** A fairly even split between keeping things running and the harder human work.
55	- **c)** Mostly the human stuff: conversations, working through conflict, helping people get aligned.
56	
57	### Q2. What people came to you for
58	
59	Picture the last few people who sought you out for something. What did they actually want?
60	
61	- **a)** Status, scheduling, a process question, where something had got to. That kind of thing.
62	- **b)** A mix. Some logistics, some heavier.
63	- **c)** Judgment, coaching, or help getting past something knotty and human.
64	
65	### Q3. The part a tool could already do
66	
67	Look at last week again, just the note-taking, the scheduling, the dashboard-updating, the status-relaying. The work a decent tool could probably handle tomorrow. How much of your week was that?
68	
69	- **a)** A big slice. More than I'd care to admit.
70	- **b)** Some, but it didn't run the week.
71	- **c)** Very little. I've mostly handed it off or stopped doing it.
72	
73	### Q4. Time spent growing people
74	
75	Think of the last time you actually sat with someone to help them grow: coaching, honest feedback, working through how they think. How much of last week looked like that?
76	
77	- **a)** Honestly, almost none. Process kept me too busy.
78	- **b)** A little, squeezed in around everything else.
79	- **c)** A real, deliberate chunk of my week.
80	
81	### Q5. Inside the ceremonies, or out in the system
82	
83	Where did your attention sit last week: inside the team's ceremonies, or out in the system around them, the impediments, the org friction, the knock-on effects nobody else is watching?
84	
85	- **a)** Almost all of it was inside the ceremonies.
86	- **b)** A bit of both.
87	- **c)** A good share was out in the wider system.
88

91	## 3. The result
92	
93	### Shared opening (everyone sees this)
94	
95	Here's the honest read. No label, no score for the wall. Just where your week actually went, and what I'd do about it if I were in your shoes.
96	
97	One thing first: almost nobody comes out of this all rising or all evaporating. Most of us are a mix, doing genuinely valuable work while a chunk of the week quietly leaks into things a tool will soon do faster and cheaper. That isn't a failure. It's just where the ground is moving, and it's far easier to move with it once you can see it.

103

114

What's true is quieter: the ground under the Scrum Master role is shifting, and the people who look clearly at where their value actually sits are the ones who'll still have a role worth doing in a few years.
116	
117	That's what I work on in [[Pragmatic AI for Agile Teams]]. If your result stung a little, that's the useful kind of sting, and it's the exact thing the course is built to help with.

196	## 5. The follow-up sequence (four emails)
197	
198	Keyed to the result. The goal is not to sell hard, it's to make the result stick and ladder gently to the course. Each subject line is a draft.
199	
200	### Email 1, sent immediately
201	
202	**Subject:** Your Scrum Master map (and the one thing I'd change)
203

215	
216	**Subject:** The most expensive hour in your week
217	
218	The status updates, the board-tidying, the note-taking. It doesn't feel expensive. It feels like the job.

# Quiz C: draft copy (for Mark to rewrite in his own voice)

**What this is:** a complete first draft of every piece of copy for Concept C, cover to follow-up emails. It's my attempt at your voice, not the final word. Rewrite freely; the design decisions underneath (five questions, concrete-recall anchoring, safe-to-admit honest answers, honest-middle result, no badge, no invented benchmark, reclaim-then-redirect move, well-positioned fallback) are the parts to preserve.

**Placeholders to fill:** the course name and links are marked `[[like this]]`. I've left the course as a placeholder because the brand-voice doc has it in flight (Pragmatic AI for Agile Teams).

**Note on the result:** it's dynamic, so I've written it as a shared scaffold plus a small library of component sentences the page assembles from your answers, then shown two fully worked examples so you can see a real result end to end.

---

## 1. The landing page (cover)

**Headline (working, under 15 words):**
Where is your Scrum Master role heading in an AI world?

**Subhead (under 25 words):**
Five honest questions about how you actually spent last week. See which parts of your role are gaining value, and which are quietly slipping away.

**The reassurance line:**
This isn't a personality quiz. There's no flattering label at the end. Just an honest read of where your work is going, and one thing to do about it.

**What you'll get (3 bullets):**
- A map of last week: the work that's rising in value, and the work a tool will soon do instead of you.
- Your single highest-leverage move, the one change worth making first.
- No archetype, no score to frame on the wall, nothing you can't act on.

**The opt-in:**
Where should I send your result?
[ email field ]
Button: **Show me my map**

Small print under the button: No spam. Unsubscribe anytime.

---

## 2. The five questions

Each question is anchored in a specific, recent memory (not "in general"), and the unflattering answer is written to be safe to pick.

### Q1. Where the week actually went

Think back over last week. When you look at where the hours really went, what took up most of them?

- **a)** Running the ceremonies and keeping the board and reports up to date. Honestly, that was most of it.
- **b)** A fairly even split between keeping things running and the harder human work.
- **c)** Mostly the human stuff: conversations, working through conflict, helping people get aligned.

### Q2. What people came to you for

Picture the last few people who sought you out for something. What did they actually want?

- **a)** Status, scheduling, a process question, where something had got to. That kind of thing.
- **b)** A mix. Some logistics, some heavier.
- **c)** Judgment, coaching, or help getting past something knotty and human.

### Q3. The part a tool could already do

Look at last week again, just the note-taking, the scheduling, the dashboard-updating, the status-relaying. The work a decent tool could probably handle tomorrow. How much of your week was that?

- **a)** A big slice. More than I'd care to admit.
- **b)** Some, but it didn't run the week.
- **c)** Very little. I've mostly handed it off or stopped doing it.

### Q4. Time spent growing people

Think of the last time you actually sat with someone to help them grow: coaching, honest feedback, working through how they think. How much of last week looked like that?

- **a)** Honestly, almost none. Process kept me too busy.
- **b)** A little, squeezed in around everything else.
- **c)** A real, deliberate chunk of my week.

### Q5. Inside the ceremonies, or out in the system

Where did your attention sit last week: inside the team's ceremonies, or out in the system around them, the impediments, the org friction, the knock-on effects nobody else is watching?

- **a)** Almost all of it was inside the ceremonies.
- **b)** A bit of both.
- **c)** A good share was out in the wider system.

---

## 3. The result

### Shared opening (everyone sees this)

Here's the honest read. No label, no score for the wall. Just where your week actually went, and what I'd do about it if I were in your shoes.

One thing first: almost nobody comes out of this all rising or all evaporating. Most of us are a mix, doing genuinely valuable work while a chunk of the week quietly leaks into things a tool will soon do faster and cheaper. That isn't a failure. It's just where the ground is moving, and it's far easier to move with it once you can see it.

### The map (assembled from the answers)

**The work that's getting more valuable, and you're already doing it:**
[list the facets scored (c) / rising]

**The work that's slipping away, a tool is coming for this:**
[list the facets scored (a) / evaporating]

### Your one move

[Reclaim sentence] [Redirect sentence]

And when you've made room, the rest worth your attention: [remaining evaporating slices, briefly].

### Where this goes next (shared close)

I'm not going to tell you AI will save your team, and I'm not going to tell you it will end your career. Both of those are stories people are selling. What's true is quieter: the ground under the Scrum Master role is shifting, and the people who look clearly at where their value actually sits are the ones who'll still have a role worth doing in a few years.

That's what I work on in [[Pragmatic AI for Agile Teams]]. If your result stung a little, that's the useful kind of sting, and it's the exact thing the course is built to help with.

[[Course link / next step]]

---

### Component library (the sentences the result assembles from)

**Q1, where the week went**
- Evaporating: "Most of your week went to running ceremonies and keeping things current. That's the part of the role a tool is coming for first."
- Rising: "Most of your week went to the hard human work: conversations, conflict, alignment. No tool does that well, and it's rising in value."

**Q2, what people came to you for**
- Evaporating: "People come to you for status and logistics. Useful, but it's exactly the errand a tool will absorb."
- Rising: "People come to you for judgment and coaching. That's a strong signal your value sits where it's hardest to replace."

**Q3, the absorbable slice**
- Evaporating: "A big slice of your week is note-taking, scheduling, and status relay, the work a tool could take tomorrow."
- Freed: "You've already shed most of the absorbable admin. That's rare, and it's what frees you for the work that matters."

**Q4, growing people**
- Evaporating: "Almost none of your week went to growing the people around you. That's the highest-value thing a Scrum Master does, and right now process is eating it."
- Rising: "You're putting real, deliberate time into growing people. That work compounds, and it's the hardest of all to automate."

**Q5, inside vs around the team**
- Evaporating: "Your attention stayed inside the ceremonies. The bigger leverage, and the harder-to-replace work, is out in the system around the team."
- Rising: "You're working the system around the team, not just the ceremonies inside it. That's where a Scrum Master actually changes outcomes."

**The move (templates)**
- Reclaim (points at the biggest evaporating slice, usually Q3): "Reclaim the time. [that block of note-taking and status relay] is the first thing to hand to a tool or simply stop doing. It's quietly the most expensive part of your week, because of what it crowds out."
- Redirect (points at the weakest rising dimension, Q2 / Q4 / Q5): "Put that time here: [sitting with people to help them grow]. It's the thinnest part of your week right now, and it's the work rising fastest in value."

**Well-positioned fallback (low evaporating, strong across the rising dimensions)**
You're the rare case. Most of your week is already in the work that's getting more valuable: the human stuff, the coaching, the system around the team. There's no admin pile to dig out of.

So your move isn't reclaiming time. It's going deeper, and helping others do the same. The Scrum Masters who thrive from here aren't just doing this work, they're getting deliberate about it and pulling their teams and peers along with them. That's the next rung.

---

## 4. Two worked examples (so you can see a whole result)

### Example A: the admin-heavy Scrum Master

*Answered: Q1 a, Q2 a, Q3 a, Q4 a, Q5 b.*

Here's the honest read. No label, no score for the wall. Just where your week actually went, and what I'd do about it if I were in your shoes.

One thing first: almost nobody comes out of this all rising or all evaporating. Most of us are a mix, doing genuinely valuable work while a chunk of the week quietly leaks into things a tool will soon do faster and cheaper. That isn't a failure. It's just where the ground is moving, and it's far easier to move with it once you can see it.

**The work that's getting more valuable, and you're already doing it:**
Not much showed up here this week, and that's the point of the map, not a verdict on you.

**The work that's slipping away, a tool is coming for this:**

- People come to you for status and logistics. Useful, but it's exactly the errand a tool will absorb.
- A big slice of your week is note-taking, scheduling, and status relay, the work a tool could take tomorrow.
- Almost none of your week went to growing the people around you. That's the highest-value thing a Scrum Master does, and right now process is eating it.

**Your one move:**
Reclaim the time. That block of note-taking and status relay is the first thing to hand to a tool or simply stop doing. It's quietly the most expensive part of your week, because of what it crowds out. Then put that time here: sitting with people to help them grow. It's the thinnest part of your week right now, and it's the work rising fastest in value.

And when you've made room, the rest worth your attention: shifting what people come to you for, and spending more time out in the system around the team.

*(then the shared "Where this goes next" close)*

### Example B: the well-positioned Scrum Master

*Answered: Q1 c, Q2 c, Q3 c, Q4 c, Q5 c.*

You're the rare case. Most of your week is already in the work that's getting more valuable: the human stuff, the coaching, the system around the team. There's no admin pile to dig out of.

So your move isn't reclaiming time. It's going deeper, and helping others do the same. The Scrum Masters who thrive from here aren't just doing this work, they're getting deliberate about it and pulling their teams and peers along with them. That's the next rung.

## 5. The follow-up sequence (four emails)

Keyed to the result. The goal is not to sell hard, it's to make the result stick and ladder gently to the course. Each subject line is a draft.

### Email 1, sent immediately

**Subject:** Your Scrum Master map (and the one thing I'd change)

Thanks for taking the quiz. Your result's below again so you don't have to go digging for it.

If you read one line twice, make it the move. Everything else can wait.

Over the next week or so I'll send you a few short notes: one on why the work that's slipping away is more expensive than it looks, one on why the human parts of your job are getting more valuable rather than less, and then I'll point you at where to take all this next. No firehose.

### Email 2, sent day 2 or 3

**Subject:** The most expensive hour in your week

The status updates, the board-tidying, the note-taking. It doesn't feel expensive. It feels like the job.

But its real cost isn't the hour it takes. It's the hour it takes away, the coaching conversation that didn't happen, the impediment nobody chased, the quiet team member nobody drew out. That's the work that actually moves a team, and it's the first thing to get squeezed when the admin piles up.

content.text:
Short answer: **Yes for the timing and delivery, with one real caveat around Email 1's personalization.** Let me break it down against what the draft actually asks for.

## What Cakemail does cleanly

**The drip mechanics (all four emails).** Cakemail's action-based automations trigger on a tag and send on relative delays: immediately, day 2–3, day 5–6, day 8–10. That maps directly onto the `aiquiz` tag the quiz already applies (this is the "nurture triggers on the tag" design already in the plan). No custom infrastructure needed — this is configured in Cakemail's UI, not the `email-automation/` CLI (that's for one-off newsletter sends).

**Emails 2, 3, and 4** are essentially evergreen/static copy. The only dynamic element is the `[soft link back to their move]` in Email 2, which has the same constraint as Email 1 below. Otherwise they drop straight in, personalized only with `[firstname]`.

## The one real caveat: Email 1's dynamic result recap

Email 1 wants `[result recap: their map + their one move]` — a variable-length, per-person assembly of rising/evaporating facets computed from the five answers. **Cakemail cannot compute this.** Merge tags only insert stored contact attributes; they can't run the quiz scoring or build variable-length lists. Same for Email 2's soft callback to "their move."

The draft already anticipates this — it's literally Open Item #3: *"Whether Email 1 should deliver the full result or a short recap plus a link back to the results page."* Two ways to resolve it:

1. **Recap + link back to the results page (recommended, low effort).** Email 1 carries a short static recap plus a link to `/quiz/{slug}/results/?...`, which already reconstructs the full map from the query string. You'd store the results URL (or its query) as a custom attribute at signup and merge it into the email. This is the cleanest fit and matches how the quiz already works.

2. **Precompute the recap and store it as a custom attribute.** Assemble the map/move text in the browser at submit time and pass it through `/api/newsletter-signup` → the Cakemail form as a custom attribute, then merge that one blob into Email 1. More integration work (extend the submission path and the form's field set), and worth remembering Cakemail's hosted-form POST *replaces* the tag set per submission (see [[reference-cakemail-form-replaces-tags]]) — attributes update the same way, so the last submission wins.

## Two things to check before building the sequence

- **Tag delivery.** The sequence keys off `aiquiz`, which is applied today. If you want tier-specific branching (e.g. divert the well-positioned "rare case" person off the evaporating-heavy framing in Emails 1–3, which otherwise misfits them), you'd re-enable the per-tier tag `aiquiz-{level}` — currently held/commented out pending confirmation that dynamically-named tags auto-create without a 422.
- **Cakemail lowercases tags** ([[reference-cakemail-lowercase-tags]]), so the automation trigger must match `aiquiz`, not `AIQuiz`.

**Bottom line:** Cakemail handles the four-email cadence and the mostly-static Emails 2–4 without trouble. The personalized map in Email 1 is the only piece it can't generate itself — go with option 1 (recap + link to the results page) and the whole sequence is straightforward.

Want me to sketch the concrete implementation for option 1 (what to store at signup and how to merge it)?

content.text: Should we be asking CakeMail for a feature request for a better version of 1?

No, I wouldn't. A feature request is the weakest path here for two reasons.

**The "better version" already exists on your side, no vendor needed.** Full result in-email (option 2) doesn't require Cakemail to build anything — it needs *you* to precompute the assembled recap in the browser (where the quiz engine already owns scoring) and store it as one custom attribute. Cakemail's existing merge tags insert it. The only thing a feature request could add is server-side conditional templating so you skip the precompute step, and that's a marginal convenience in exchange for a dependency on someone else's roadmap and timeline. You already own the assembly logic; keep owning it.

**A solo-operator feature request to an ESP is low-leverage.** It lands on Cakemail's schedule, not yours, and "dynamic conditional content blocks" is a big ask that touches their template engine — the kind of thing that sits in a backlog for a year or never ships. Betting a content pipeline on that is worse than the client-side path you can build this week.

**But the real question is whether you even need the better version yet.** The gap between "recap + link to results page" (option 1) and "full result in email" (option 2) is one click. Ship option 1 first, then look at whether people actually click through to the results page. If click-through is healthy, option 1 is fine and option 2 buys you nothing. If it's poor *and* you think the missing full result is why, then build option 2 yourself. That's the "what action would we take?" test — don't invest in richer personalization (vendor-built or self-built) until you have a number saying the simple version is leaking.

So: skip the feature request, ship option 1, measure, and only reach for option 2 (self-built) if the data says the click is costing you.
